children: By Avinash  P

Turkish stocks steadied on Thursday after a sharp selloff as policymakers sought to calm investors rattled by liquidity concerns linked to new fund regulations, while emerging market currencies clawed back some lost ground against the dollar.

Turkey's main stock index had dropped more than 5% on Wednesday, renewing scrutiny of the country's capital markets and raising concerns that liquidity strains at a handful of funds could spread more broadly through the financial system.

The Financial Stability Committee, the country's top coordinating body for financial-sector risks and crisis response, on Thursday said that recent volatility posed no fundamental or structural risk to the functioning of the domestic capital markets.
Turkey's central bank announced measures to support market functioning, including one-week repo auctions, revising banks' borrowing limits and reducing collateral haircuts.
The benchmark BIST-100 index
rose 1.1%, while the main banking index (.XBANK) jumped 5.9% after losing 6.4% on Wednesday.

"The true extent of interconnected lending and collateral and potential contagion is always hard to predict, but this does not appear to have much to do with macroeconomic conditions and should not create systemic risk," said Hasnain Malik, head of geopolitical risk and emerging-market equity strategy research at Tellimer in Dubai.

Turkey's Capital Markets Board said it filed criminal complaints against 38 people and barred them from trading on Borsa Istanbul for two years over their alleged share manipulation, a move which investors viewed as an effort to stabilise equity markets.
Stocks elsewhere across developing economies were mixed, with the broader MSCI's index tracking equities
CBOE:EFS
flat.
In South Africa, local stocks
inched 0.3% higher, helped by stronger commodity prices including gold and platinum
which are the key exports from the country.
DOLLAR STALLS
In currencies, the US dollar stalled after jumping to a seven-week high following the Federal Reserve's move to hike interest rates for the first time in three years and striking a hawkish tone.
Oil prices fell further, helping lift several EM currencies, including the South African rand
that was up 0.7% after having weakened to a more-than one-month low of 16.408 a dollar in the previous session.
The Hungarian forint
edged 0.4% higher to 317.33 per dollar, having touched a two-week low on Wednesday.
But many expect the relief to fade.

"A stronger US dollar is likely to keep weighing on EM currencies, outweighing the late-session decline in gas prices and leaving the overall balance tilted to the downside," Francesco Pesole, FX strategist at ING, said in a note.
INVESTORS EYE CZECH RATE DECISION

In Central and Eastern Europe, focus turned to the Czech central bank's rate decision later in the day. Investors expect benchmark rates to be held steady at 3.75%, with its main repo rate sufficiently above inflation.
Stocks in Prague
gained 0.5%, while the koruna
weakened 0.1% against the euro.
Both South Africa and Hungary's central banks are set to announce their monetary policy decisions next week.
